ai.title: Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Inhaled Aspergillus spores cause a spectrum of lung disease, from allergic inflammation to invasive infection, especially in patients with chronic lung disease or immunosuppression. Diagnosis relies on clinical, radiologic and microbiologic clues, often limited in low‑resource settings.

b: Caused by Aspergillus fumigatus complex, ubiquitous in soil and decaying vegetation.
Risk factors: asthma/COPD, prior TB, HIV, malnutrition, prolonged steroids, chemotherapy.
sections.p: Bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (BPA) describes any Aspergillus‑related lung disease. It ranges from allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) in asthmatics to chronic cavitary disease and acute invasive infection in immunocompromised hosts.

b: ABPA: IgE‑mediated hypersensitivity, central bronchiectasis, fleeting infiltrates.
Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA): >3 months symptoms, cavities with fungal balls, low‑grade inflammation.
Invasive aspergillosis (IA): rapid tissue invasion, haemorrhage, high mortality.
sections.p: Think of BPA as a problem of host immunity versus fungal load. The disease phenotype follows the balance: intact immunity → allergic response; partial immunity → chronic cavitary disease; severe immunosuppression → invasive disease.

b: ABPA often mimics uncontrolled asthma; look for brown‑ish mucus plugs.
CPA may be mistaken for post‑TB cavities; note progressive symptoms >3 months.
IA presents with fever, pleuritic chest pain, and new infiltrates in neutropenic patients.
sections.p: Patients present with cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, and worsening dyspnoea. In low‑resource hospitals, differentiate BPA from TB relapse, bacterial pneumonia, and lung cancer.

t.b: What is the pattern of lung involvement? – Shows infiltrates, cavitation, or fungal ball; may be normal early in IA.
What are the detailed radiologic features? – Central bronchiectasis in ABPA, thick‑walled cavity with aspergilloma in CPA, halo sign in IA.
Does the patient have an allergic response? – >1000 IU/mL supports ABPA; normal in CPA/IA.
Is there sensitisation or chronic exposure? – Positive IgE in ABPA; elevated IgG in CPA.

t.a: Sputum or broncho‑alveolar lavage (BAL) microscopy & culture
t.b: Is the fungus present? – Hyphae on microscopy or growth of Aspergillus confirms infection; culture may be unavailable, rely on microscopy.
Is there invasive disease? – Positive in IA; may be false‑negative in low‑resource labs, use clinical picture.

b: ABPA: oral corticosteroids to suppress hypersensitivity; add itraconazole if steroids alone insufficient.
CPA: oral itraconazole (first line) or voriconazole; surgery for massive haemoptysis or solitary aspergilloma.
IA: intravenous voriconazole (first‑line); avoid amphotericin B in renal failure; consider combination therapy in refractory cases.
sections.p: Treat the underlying immune defect, then use antifungal therapy tailored to disease type. Supportive care includes airway clearance and monitoring for haemorrhage.

b: Assuming all cavitary lesions are TB – check for fungal ball and IgG.
Starting steroids without confirming ABPA – can worsen CPA or IA.
Relying solely on negative culture – microscopy and serology are essential.
sections.p: Misattributing symptoms to TB or asthma leads to delayed therapy and higher mortality.

b: ABPA: asthma + elevated IgE + central bronchiectasis.
CPA: >3 months symptoms + cavity + Aspergillus IgG.
IA: neutropenia + fever + halo sign + positive galactomannan.
sections.p: Examiners test integration of history, radiology and immunology.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid respiratory deterioration in a neutropenic patient
Persistent fever despite antibiotics in an immunocompromised host
